text:
Odysseus steps forward with a bowl of wine and offers it to the giant.

The wine came from Maron, a priest of Apollo, whose household drank it mixed with twenty parts of water to one.

The giant drinks three bowls, and Homer counts them.

Then he asks the guest's name, and promises a present.

Odysseus tells him his name is Nobody.

The giant laughs and says that his present will be this: he will eat Nobody last.

A name like that is a joke, and the giant is the only one who does not hear it.

It is a small trick, and the whole escape will hang on it.

The giant sinks to the floor and passes out.

Odysseus looks at the sleeping giant, then at his men, and nods.

Odysseus pushes the stake into the fire and holds it there until the point glows.

No one speaks, because no one needs to.

Then he and four men lift it and put it in the giant's eye.

The cave fills with a sound that is not quite a roar.

Homer reaches for a blacksmith's simile: an axe plunged into cold water, hissing.

The giant's scream brings his neighbours to the cave.

They ask if someone is killing him.

He shouts back that Nobody is killing him, by trickery and not by force.

The neighbours reply that if nobody is hurting him, it must be a sickness from Zeus.

He should pray to his father and let them sleep.

They go home, and the trick has worked.

The giant has lost his eye, but he has not lost his strength, and the stone still waits at the door.
